name: Snowdrops
title: When to plant snowdrop bulbs in the UK
heading: When to plant snowdrop bulbs
summary: Dry bulbs in October and November, or in the green in February and March. In the green is the more reliable method.
description: When to plant snowdrop bulbs in the UK: dry bulbs in October and November, or in the green in February and March. Depth and spacing included.
card: In the green, February to March
answer: Plant snowdrop bulbs in the UK in one of two ways. Dry bulbs go in during autumn: [Gardeners' World](https://www.gardenersworld.com/how-to/grow-plants/how-to-grow-snowdrops/) gives October and November, and says dry bulbs are tricky to establish. The [RHS growing guide](https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/snowdrops/growing-guide) says they are very prone to drying out, so buy them as soon as they are available and plant them immediately.

The more reliable method is planting in the green: plants lifted just after flowering, while the leaves are still green. The [RHS February flowers notes](https://www.rhs.org.uk/advice/in-month/february/flowers) list dividing and planting snowdrops in the green, and the [March notes](https://www.rhs.org.uk/advice/in-month/march/flowers) say to do it then if you missed February. Gardeners' World gives February and March as well.

answerNote: Plant dry bulbs about 10cm deep, pointed end up. Plant snowdrops in the green at the same depth they were growing before, which you can see where the stem turns from green to white, and at least 10cm apart. Those figures are from [Gardens Illustrated](https://www.gardensillustrated.com/plants/bulbs/how-to-grow-snowdrops). The RHS also says to replant at the same depth.
intro: Snowdrops break the usual bulb rule. Most spring bulbs are bought dry and planted in autumn. Snowdrops can be planted that way, but they dry out easily and often fail. The RHS puts freshly lifted plants, set in when the foliage is just dying back in late spring, first. Next best is buying them just after flowering, still in leaf. Dry bulbs are the fallback.
If you are reading this in autumn, plant any dry bulbs the day you buy them. If you can wait, order plants in the green for after they flower.

calendar.label: Plant in the green
calendar.detail: Just after flowering, while the leaves are still green. The RHS lists this for February, and for March if you missed it. Gardeners' World gives February and March.

calendar.label: Plant dry bulbs
calendar.detail: Gardeners' World names October and November. Gardens Illustrated says autumn, at the same time as daffodils. The RHS says buy dry bulbs as soon as they appear and plant them immediately.

calendar.label: In flower
calendar.detail: The RHS calls them among the first plants to flower in the new year. Gardeners' World says they bloom as early as January and February. Gardens Illustrated says most flower in late winter and early spring.

timing: For dry bulbs, the named months are October and November. Gardeners' World says plant them in those months, and that this method is tricky. The RHS does not give a later deadline: it says buy them as soon as they are available and plant immediately, because the bulbs dry out. Gardens Illustrated puts dry bulbs in during autumn, alongside daffodils.

In the green is February and March. The RHS February advice is to divide and plant bulbs in the green, including snowdrops. If that month passes, the March advice is to do it then. Gardeners' World says lift plants just after flowering and before the foliage turns yellow, and that established clumps can be divided after flowering in March or April.
The RHS also describes a third moment: planting freshly lifted snowdrops when the foliage is just dying back in late spring. It calls that the best way to establish them.
where: The RHS says to plant in partial shade, in moist but well-drained soil, with leafmould or garden compost worked in. The soil must not dry out in summer. Its plant guide says snowdrops grow in most soils apart from permanently wet ground, and that they dislike very dry, sandy soil in full sun.

Gardeners' World suggests the foot of a deciduous hedge, or beneath deciduous shrubs, where there is light and rain in late winter and cover in summer. On heavy soil, it says add a little sharp sand or grit to the planting hole.
planting: Separate a bundle of snowdrops in the green and replant straight away. Gardens Illustrated says to use the colour change on the stem, green above and white below, as the depth mark, and to leave at least 10cm between plants. Water after planting. The RHS says clumps can also be split and planted singly at the same depth they were growing.

Dry bulbs go in pointed end up. Gardens Illustrated says about 10cm deep. Do not store them in the bag while you wait for a free afternoon. The RHS says squirrels may dig up dry bulbs, and Gardeners' World suggests a chicken-wire cover until the leaves show, then taking it off.
pots: Snowdrops grow in pots, but Gardeners' World says they suffer if the compost dries out in summer and that they need repotting every year. Gardens Illustrated says to repot into fresh compost while they are dormant, in late spring or summer, and to keep the compost moist all year.
aftercare: Once snowdrops are settled they need little care. The RHS says there is nothing to prune: let the foliage die back naturally. Every few years, lift and divide congested clumps as the leaves turn yellow, split them with as little damage as you can, and replant at the same depth.

problems.title: Dry bulbs that never come up
text: The usual cause is bulbs that dried out before they rooted. Gardeners' World calls dry bulbs tricky to establish. Plant in the green next time, or plant dry bulbs on the day you buy them.

problems.title: Squirrels and grey mould
text: The RHS notes that squirrels may dig up snowdrops planted as dry bulbs, and that grey mould can affect snowdrops in mild winters. Gardens Illustrated says grey mould is also a problem in very wet, poorly drained soil, and that affected bulbs should be binned so it does not spread.

faqs.question: Is it too late to plant snowdrop bulbs in November?
answer: No. November is inside the dry-bulb window Gardeners' World gives, which is October and November. Plant them the day you get them. The RHS says dry snowdrop bulbs are very prone to drying out, so a bulb left in the bag is the bigger risk.

faqs.question: Is it too late to plant snowdrop bulbs in December?
answer: December is later than the October and November window in the Gardeners' World guide. If the bulbs are still firm, the RHS advice for any bulb you meant to plant earlier is to get it into the ground or a pot now, rather than storing it until next autumn, and to discard any that are soft or rotten. Expect dry bulbs planted this late to be less reliable than snowdrops planted in the green in February, or in March if you missed February.

faqs.question: What does in the green mean?
answer: Snowdrops lifted after flowering while they are still in leaf, then replanted straight away. The RHS and Gardeners' World both treat this as more reliable than dry bulbs.
